The challenge remains that while any one diplomatic headline hope is very unlikely to amount to much, the market's base case remains that this will end via some kind of deal.

So while this likely isn't the end, this is what the end will likely look like and you gotta kinda act accordingly so you don't get run over as this latest episode runs its course. 

Stay alive (and keep your job) to buy back on the other side if this once again isn't the one.

Another month in the books. Here’s the October post-mortem.

As most of you know, after printing huge over the summer, September took a massive bite out of me when my long bond trade completely blew up. Personally i ate nearly a cool $1M drawdown, and the firm’s book suffered.

Scrambling for a redemption trade, I turned my guns toward crude. Anyone paying attention knows the sharp, non-lazy observers were already flagging the uptick in Strait of Hormuz transit volumes back in August.

Naturally the lazy tourist crowd—you know exactly which bald frauds and their entourage I’m talking about—along with the sell side echo chamber, didn't start foaming at the mouth over that transit spike until late September.

I saw the window to fade that midwit consensus and began building a massive long crude in late September. Having missed the summer oil rip bc i was married to that dead bond trade, this felt like my shot to front-run the second leg higher.

Inventory buffers were bone dry, Iranian and Kuwaiti barrels were still knocked offline, and we were tracking the unmistakable return of Chinese physical buying. Fading the street consensus was a no-brainer. That said i still think right now is an absolute suicide mission for retail to touch crude.

This tape is dictated almost entirely by asymmetric, paywalled data, opaque physic dynamics, and dirty freight runs. For a retail punter trying to track those micro-mechanics solo, you're just asking to get chopped to pieces. Tread lightly.

Anyway concurrent with that, i started building a short NQ in early October, which paid off handsomely last week. Heading into the midterms, I’ve started aggressively taking chips off the table. 

Personally i still see upside skew on crude post-election—i peg the odds of a kinetic escalation at 50% minimum. But trading discipline dictates degrossing and deleveraging into massive binary event risk. I locked in the PnL and will spend the next 48 hours hunting for cleaner re-entry.

While I’m still letting a residual oil long ride, i completely flatlined the NQ short. That bounce off the 200dma looks greasy, and as Le Shrub famously quipped, you never want to step in front of the degenerate retail bid in this "Golden Age of Fraud."

More importantly the ultimate catalyst: my favorite walking, talking human indicator. A Korean guy—hands down the single most toxic, reverse-Midas clown i have ever witnessed in my life, yet struts around convinced he’s God’s gift to the markets.

Word reached my desk that this absolute midwit panic-vomited his entire US equity book on Friday. You simply do not ignore an oracle print like that. Rather than trying to be a hero and frontrun the tape, I’d rather wait for confirmation and chase momentum.

Riding into the midterms holding nothing but residual oil length. Best of luck out there folks!

CBOT Corn suffers worst monthly decline in more than three years as hedge funds liquidate longs

Corn futures slumped 10% in October, their worst monthly performance since June 2023, falling to a three-and-a-half-month low near USD 4.50 per bushel. The total decline of 16.7% in the past two months marks a sharp reversal from the three-year high in early September around USD 5.50, driven by US harvest pressure, weaker export data and hopes that a Black Sea truce could ease regional supply disruptions and improve export flows.

The US corn harvest was 60% complete as of 25 October, while weekly export figures from the US Department of Agriculture showed a nearly 15% decline. Adding to the downside pressure has been aggressive selling by wrong-footed hedge funds, which built a record net long position of 431,000 contracts, equivalent to 2.2 billion bushels, during August in anticipation of further price gains.

By the latest COT reporting week to 27 October, that position had collapsed to just 56,000 contracts, representing a reduction of 87% and highlighting the scale of long liquidation over the past five weeks.

While the sharp reduction in speculative length may eventually help stabilise prices as selling pressure fades, the near-term outlook remains challenged by seasonal supply pressure, uncertain export demand and developments in the Black Sea region. A sustained recovery will likely require evidence of stronger physical demand or a renewed supply-side concern.

#Commodities:
Oil: Brent trades down 3% with the January contract at USD 110 after trading above USD 114 on Friday. The latest decline came amid reports that President Trump favours giving diplomacy with Iran more time before potentially resuming strikes after Tuesday’s US midterm elections. Qatari and Iranian officials continued talks, although attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz highlighted persistent supply risks. Meanwhile, OPEC+ kept output targets unchanged through December, while Goldman Sachs raised its Brent forecast to USD 105 for December and an average of USD 88 in 2027, citing heightened geopolitical risks in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Precious metals: Gold rebounds 1% to USD 3,915 after Friday’s break below key support, now resistance, at USD 3,970 drove prices to a one-year low, leaving October down 6.8%. The selloff, fuelled by momentum selling and long liquidation, was exacerbated by the rout in AI stocks and rising energy prices. While structural support for gold in our opinion remains intact, market sentiment and positioning may need to stabilise before these drivers regain influence. For now, the focus remains on global equities, Middle East developments, energy prices and US rate expectations. Silver, which led last week’s selloff, rebounds 2.3% to USD 50.20, with traders watching for signs of stabilisation or renewed selling.

Copper trades higher at USD 6.52 following a two-day correction driven by some of the same forces that weighed on precious metals, notably weakness in AI-related stocks that raised doubts about projected data centre demand. While sluggish Chinese manufacturing remains a concern, prices are finding support from growing signs of mine supply constraints. Meanwhile, premiums paid by Chinese importers over LME prices have reached record highs, signalling tightness in the world’s largest copper refining market.
